intro.html: English has a whole toolbox of words for how hard something is, and each tool does a different job. A climb can be arduous, a duty onerous, a copying job laborious, a race grueling. A rival can be formidable, a box cumbersome, a ladder precarious. And some tasks are hopeless (futile) or much too easy (facile).

Hard work: arduous (steep, demanding), onerous (a heavy burden), laborious (slow and painstaking), grueling (exhausting). Hard to face or handle: formidable, cumbersome, precarious. No use: futile. Easy: effortless (praise) and facile (usually blame).
The Latin inside helps: arduus meant steep, onus a load, labor work, formido fear, and facilis easy.

words.def: needing great effort; hard and tiring
words.ex: The {arduous} climb took six hours, almost all of it uphill.
words.ctx: Restoring the old ship was {arduous}: volunteers spent four winters scraping, sanding and replacing every rotten plank by hand.

mn.text: The trail rises like a wall, and Tia and Marcus puff up it one step at a time: the climb is {arduous}.

scene.alt: Two sweating hikers with backpacks trudge up a steep mountain trail.

words.def: heavy and troublesome, like a burden
words.ex: Caring for twelve goats turned out to be an {onerous} chore.
words.ctx: The new rules were so {onerous} that small shops could barely follow them; each one demanded hours of extra paperwork every week.
words.etym: From Latin onerosus, from onus (load, burden).
words.note: Onerous has nothing to do with honor; think of onus, a load.

mn.text: Every box in the move lands on us: Sven staggers along under a tower of them. The job is {onerous}.

scene.alt: A big man staggers under a tall stack of heavy boxes.

words.def: needing a lot of slow, careful work
words.ex: Copying the old recipe book by hand was a {laborious} job.
words.ctx: Before computers, making a dictionary was {laborious}; editors wrote each definition on a paper slip and sorted millions of slips by hand.
words.etym: From Latin laboriosus, from labor (work, toil).

mn.text: Felix copies the whole thick book by hand with a feather pen, one slow letter at a time: the work is {laborious}.

scene.alt: A tired man copies a thick book by hand with a feather pen.

words.ex: After a {grueling} practice in the heat, the team flopped onto the grass.
words.ctx: The race was {grueling}: fifty miles over rocky trails, through rain and wind, with only two short stops for food.

mn.cue: too tired for anything but GRUEL
mn.text: After hiking up and down three mountains, Jonah is too tired to eat anything but a bowl of mush, called gruel: the hike was {grueling}.

scene.alt: An exhausted teen slumps by a campfire with a bowl of mush after a long hike.

words.def: inspiring fear or respect through size, strength or difficulty
words.ex: The chess champion was a {formidable} opponent.
words.ctx: With its steep walls, deep moat and towering gate, the castle presented a {formidable} obstacle to anyone hoping to get inside.
words.etym: From Latin formidabilis, from formidare (to fear), from formido (fear).

mn.cue: FORM-idable: a FORM so big you fear it
mn.text: The dragon guarding the gate is huge, fast and clever, and even brave Maya takes a deep breath: it is a {formidable} foe.

scene.alt: A girl in a helmet holds up a shield before a huge, smoking dragon guarding a castle.

words.def: large and awkward to carry or use; also, slow and complicated
words.ex: The {cumbersome} old suitcase had no wheels and kept banging into my knees.
words.ctx: The sign-up process was {cumbersome}: families had to fill out four forms, mail them separately and then call to confirm each one.

mn.text: Pip tries to carry a huge piece of lumber home by himself, but it is so long and heavy that he can barely shuffle: it is {cumbersome}.

scene.alt: A boy staggers while carrying a huge, awkward log.

words.def: unsteady and likely to fall or fail
words.ex: The cat sat in a {precarious} spot on the very edge of the shelf.
words.ctx: After the storm washed away half the trail, the hikers’ path along the cliff became {precarious}, with loose rocks sliding at every step.
words.etym: From Latin precarius, “got by begging, uncertain,” from precari (to pray, beg): what you hold only by someone’s favor can be taken away at any moment.

mn.text: Dev carries a wobbling tower of twelve plates across the kitchen. Take care! It could crash at any moment: the stack is {precarious}.

scene.alt: A teen carries a tall, wobbling tower of plates that looks ready to fall.

words.def: useless; having no chance of success
words.ex: Trying to stay dry in that storm was {futile}.
words.ctx: Every attempt to fix the old radio proved {futile}; no matter which part they replaced, it still made nothing but static.

mn.cue: FUTILE = leaky: filling a bucket full of holes
mn.text: Grandpa Gus keeps pouring water into a bucket full of holes, and it runs out as fast as it goes in: his effort is {futile}.

scene.alt: A grandfather pours water into a bucket that leaks it all out again.

words.def: too simple to be useful; shallow and easy
words.ex: The essay offered a {facile} answer to a hard question.
words.ctx: Her critics called the plan {facile}: it promised to fix the city’s traffic jams simply by painting new lines, ignoring every deeper problem.
words.etym: From Latin facilis, “easy to do,” from facere (to do).
words.note: Facile can also mean done with ease (a facile writer), but it is most often a criticism.

mn.text: Asked how to save the old theater, Rex says, “Just tell people to come!”, as if it were that simple. His answer is {facile}.

scene.alt: At a meeting, a man offers an oversimple answer while two others facepalm and frown.

words.def: needing, or seeming to need, no effort at all
words.ex: The dancer made the high leap look {effortless}.
words.ctx: After years of practice, Maya’s piano playing seemed {effortless}, though anyone who had heard her first lessons knew how hard she had worked.

mn.text: Pip puffs halfway up the ladder, but the cat springs straight onto the top shelf in one smooth leap: for her it is {effortless}.

scene.alt: A boy struggles up a ladder while a cat leaps easily to the top of a bookshelf.

after.html: facile sounds like praise (it shares a root with facility, ease), but it is usually a criticism: a facile answer is too easy to be any good. If you mean easy in a good way, choose effortless. And onerous (a burden, from onus) has nothing to do with honor.

after.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: The skater’s spins looked {effortless}, though she had practiced them every morning for six years.

after.cap: Easy in a good way, graceful: effortless.

items.q: A critic writes: “The book offers a ______ solution to a deep problem; it is far too simple.” Which word fits?
items.why: Facile is a criticism: too simple to be useful. Effortless is praise for making something hard look easy.

items.q: True or false: an onerous task is one that brings great honor.
items.why: False. Onerous comes from onus, a load: an onerous task is a heavy burden.

items.q: Trying to blow out the sun like a birthday candle would be…
items.why: It has no chance of working at all, so it is futile.

choices: The vase sat in a precarious spot on the edge of the table.
The precarious nap left him refreshed.
She gave a precarious smile of welcome.
items.why: Precarious means unsteady and likely to fall or fail, like a vase on the very edge.
